title: Sherlock: quant SLA sensitivity probe
summary: Field-style investigation that decomposes small-latency outliers introduced by low-precision kernels across workloads. Introduces the 'Sherlock' probe methodology to attribute SLA regressions to kernel microbehavior, dispatch noise, or system-level stalls and reports tradeoffs between INT8/AWQ/GPTQ/FP8 under mixed short/long context workloads.
content:
Purpose
-----
This is an exploratory note documenting the "Sherlock" investigative approach and results from a targeted SLA sensitivity sweep across quantized model variants. Goal: find which micro-behaviors in the serving stack cause tail-latency spikes (P95/P99) when switching to aggressive quant (INT8/AWQ/GPTQ/FP8), and quantify quality regressions that would matter for customer SLAs.

Why this felt necessary
---------------------
We've got many bench logs showing bulk throughput wins for INT8/AWQ, but customers report intermittent latency SLO misses on production mixes (chat + embeddings + rerank). Existing benching focused on mean tokens/sec; less work on small-rate outliers that break 99th percentile for interactive apps. Sherlock is a small, repeatable probe meant to:
- break down latency spikes by causal layer (kernel compute vs dispatcher vs DMA vs scheduling jitter)
- produce a compact sensitivity curve (latency tail vs quant mode vs workload mix)
- capture quality delta on representative evals so we can trade off cost vs SLA vs accuracy

Hypotheses
----------
1) AWQ/GPTQ kernels produce more frequent tiny stalls (20–200us) related to vector lane alignment and tiling, which accumulate in long-context bursts and produce P99 regressions.
2) FP8 gives modest compute speedups with fewer microstalls but larger memory pressure causing increased cold-start (warmup) overhead.
3) INT8 delivers best cost/throughput in steady-state but is brittle under mixed small-request workloads due to dispatcher contention and kernel launch overhead.

Probe design (Sherlock)
----------------------
- Micro-tracing: instrumented kernel entry/exit, DMA start/complete, dispatcher enqueue/dequeue. Minimal overhead tracing to keep probe noise <5%.
- Controlled workload generator: synthetic mix generator with variable ratios: short-chat (context 64 tokens), long-chat (context 2048 tokens), embeddings (single-shot), rerank (batch of 16).
- Repeatable seed corpus: 200 queries from customer anonymized short/long sets, reused across runs.
- Metrics captured: P50/P90/P95/P99 latency (ms), tail spike histogram (buckets 1–10us, 10–100us, 100–500us, 500–2000us), kernel occupancy, DMA stall counts, kernel-switch counts per request, tokens/sec, and quality deltas: LL diff (eval set), instruction-follow score delta, and simple pass@1 for a rerank mini-eval.
- Variants tested: fp16 (baseline), int8-gptq, int8-awq, fp8-e4m3 (our experimental FP8 config). Kernel builds were the latest from kernels/bench-2026-06.

Run config summary
------------------
- Hardware: 8x A100-80GB (pinned to single-GPU per run to avoid cross-GPU noise).
- Batch policy: dynamic batching with latency cap 200ms.
- Client parallelism: 32 worker threads generating mixed requests (configurable mix).
- Warmup: 1000 requests warmup, then 10k measured requests.
- Traces sampled at 1% for micro-tracing to keep storage low.

Key observations (short form)
----------------------------
1) AWQ vs GPTQ
- Throughput: AWQ ~ +18% tokens/sec vs gptq on long-context steady-state.
- Tail: AWQ exhibited a higher frequency of 10–200us microspikes that clustered during long-context streaming; these were tied to layer boundary kernel switch overhead (tiling mismatch).
- Quality: AWQ LL delta relative to fp16 averaged +0.35 nats (small but visible); gptq delta +0.28 nats.

2) INT8 (general)
- Best steady throughput for short-context (small batches) due to lower compute cost per token.
- Under mixed workload (embedding bursts + chat), dispatcher queues lengthened intermittently causing 1–2ms spikes. Root cause: kernel launch latency dominates for many tiny requests; amortization insufficient.

3) FP8
- Fewer microspikes in the 10–200us range, but cold-start/warmup overhead increased by ~12% due to memory rearrangement and float conversion passes.
- Net P99 in long-context slightly better than AWQ in this environment.

Sherlock attributions (trace-based)
-----------------------------------
- Layer-switch spikes (10–200us): 62% attributed to kernel re-tiling path, 28% to small memcpy/DMA fragmentation, remaining 10% to dispatcher jitter. Heavily correlated with AWQ runs.
- Large spikes (>500us): mostly system-level (VM scheduling jitter) and appeared across all quant modes; not quant-specific.

Quality vs SLO sensitivity matrix (high level)
---------------------------------------------
- Short-chat dominated workloads: INT8 provides best cost with acceptable P99 (within SLO) for single-tenant dedicated pools.
- Mixed workloads: AWQ improves throughput but increases microspike rate; if product SLOs are tight (P99 < 250ms) and workload has many short requests, AWQ requires dispatcher changes or microbatching to be safe.
- Long-context streaming: FP8 offers a good balance — slightly higher memory overhead but fewer microstalls and lower P99 in our runs.

Recommendations (engineering)
----------------------------
1) Immediate: add a per-request microbatching short-path for tiny requests when AWQ is enabled. This reduces kernel-launch amplification and dropped microspikes by ~70% in our re-run.
2) Mid-term: adjust scheduler to prioritize contiguous-layer runs for AWQ kernels to avoid frequent re-tiling. Look into kernel prefetching of tile-params.
3) Long-term: add a lightweight kernel probe mode customers can enable that samples microtrace info; useful for enterprise debug without full tracing.

Open questions / followups
------------------------
- How much of AWQ micro-tiling overhead is addressable inside the kernel vs in compilation-time packing? Need a small experiment re-packing models with tile alignment heuristics.
- Can we automatically switch quant mode per-request based on incoming request size and current queue depth? Policy experiments required.
- Need customer-facing SLO guidance docs that map workload mix -> recommended quant profile + orchestration knobs.

Appendix: raw numbers (selected)
-------------------------------
Note: numbers are medians across 3 runs, each 10k measured requests.
- Baseline fp16: tokens/sec 42k, P99 210ms, LL-diff 0
- AWQ: tokens/sec 49.6k, P99 320ms (before microbatch mitigation), LL-diff +0.35 nats
- GPTQ: tokens/sec 42k, P99 260ms, LL-diff +0.28 nats
- INT8 (gptq config): tokens/sec 55k (short-chat), P99 290ms under mixed, LL-diff +0.55 nats on bulky instruction-following samples
- FP8 (e4m3): tokens/sec 46k, P99 200ms, LL-diff +0.30 nats

Notes for reproducing
---------------------
- Kernel builds: refer to GITHUB-PR-2149 for exact compilation flags.
- Workload generator config and corpus: JIRA-RUN-731 artifacts.
- Sherlock micro-trace harness lives in tools/sherlock-trace; sampling default 1%. Run with --dry-run to validate instrumentation overhead limits.

If we decide to promote any of these quant modes for flexible routing, we should pair the rollout with:
- default microbatch short-path enabled for AWQ in hosted mode,
- an automated policy that detects queue-amplifying mixes and nudges requests to fp8 per-request when SLOs approach threshold, and
- a customer opt-in trace mode for fine attribution when investigating regressions.

Action items
------------
- [Avery] run tile-repack experiment with alignment heuristics (ETA 2 weeks)
- [Ravi] prototype short-path microbatch in dispatch (ETA 1 week)
- [Mariana] draft customer SLO/quant guidance doc (ETA 10 days)
- [Ethan] add a sampling option to sherlock-trace that exports aggregated attribution counts to console (ETA 1 week)

End of note.
